title: Physiological intensity profile, exercise load and performance predictors of a 65-km mountain ultra-marathon
authors: Fornasiero A, Savoldelli A, Fruet D, Boccia G, Pellegrini B, Schena F
population: Twenty-three amateur trail runners in a 65 km mountain ultra-marathon (4000 m ascent), HR monitored
findings: Mean race intensity 77.1+/-4.4% of HRmax, distributed 85.7+/-19.4% zone I, 13.9+/-18.6% zone II, 0.4+/-0.9% zone III (zones defined by VT1 and VT2).
Exercise load 766+/-110 TRIMP units; race time 11.8+/-1.6 h.
Race time correlated with VO2max (r=-0.66) and PMax (r=-0.73); thresholds did not improve prediction; laboratory variables explained only 59% of race-time variance.
Authors state results support VT1 as a boundary of tolerable intensity in such events.
Mean race intensity was 77.1% +/- 4.4% of HRmax, distributed as 85.7% in Zone I (below VT1), 13.9% in Zone II (VT1-VT2) and 0.4% in Zone III (above VT2).
Exercise load was 766 +/- 110 TRIMP units; race time was 11.8 +/- 1.6 h.
Race time correlated negatively with VO2max (r = -0.66, P < 0.001) and peak power (r = -0.73, P < 0.001); exercise thresholds did not improve prediction.
Laboratory variables explained only 59% of race-time variance; the authors suggest VT1 is a boundary of tolerable intensity in such events.
limitations: One race, amateur sample, observational and about racing not training. Extrapolation to 100-mile events untested.
implications: Ultra race-day pacing: spend the large majority of the race below VT1/LT1; use that as the zone 1 anchor for ultra-specific sessions.
Prioritise time on feet and low-intensity volume for ultra goals (inference; no TID trial exists in ultra runners).
Anchor ultra race pacing guidance to heart rate at or below VT1 for most of the event (about 86% of time in Zone I in this race) and flag planned effort above VT2 as a risk.
The paper does not describe training intensity distribution, so any easy-running share in training is an engine choice, not a finding.

Compute TRIMP or an equivalent from watch heart-rate data as a race-load estimate (about 770 units for a 12 h mountain ultra) and use it to scale the post-race recovery block; the scaling rule is an engine choice.

verification.notes: Crossref: online 2017-09-04, print 2018-06. Numbers confirmed in abstract. The training-emphasis implication is flagged as inference.
